extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television fans, and researchers seeking information about the sitcom 30 Rock
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style article describing the American satirical surreal sitcom 30 Rock: its premise, production, cast, episodes, stylistic features, reception, and awards. The page summarizes how the series was made, notable creative choices, and its critical/industry recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed genres: Sitcom; Satire; Surreal comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly describes 30 Rock as an American satirical surrealist sitcom and frames expectations about tone and comedic approach (e.g., surreal humor used to parody corporate structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise / setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Set behind the scenes of a fictional live sketch comedy show (TGS with Tracy Jordan) located at 30 Rockefeller Plaza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The premise orients character relationships and recurring storylines (Liz Lemon as head writer, Jack Donaghy as network executive, etc.) and establishes the workplace-comedy framework that shapes episode content and satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody and corporate satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Known for its use of parody to satirize the corporate structure of NBC and its parent companies (General Electric and Comcast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The show fictionalizes real events (e.g., acquisition by Comcast as Kabletown) and uses corporate parody as a recurring comedic target; this is presented as a defining creative approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal humor and 'live-action cartoon' style
rubrics_metrics.description: Described as 'a live-action cartoon' and noted for use of surreal humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites surreal humor as a tonal descriptor that informs the show's frequent non-realist gags and plot beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive use of cutaways, sight gags, and breaking the fourth wall
rubrics_metrics.description: The show was influential in its extensive use of cutaways, sight gags, and breaking the fourth wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stylistic devices are highlighted as central to the series' comedic language and timing (examples and descriptions appear throughout the article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Production format: single-camera setup (with multi-camera live exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most 30 Rock episodes were produced in a single-camera setup; two live episodes were produced in multi-camera format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The production choice is tied to the show's look/feel; exceptions (live broadcast episodes) are explicitly noted and discussed in the production/episodes sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running time and episode structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Running time: 22 minutes. Series format: episodic seasons with story arcs developing over seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Season and episode counts (7 seasons, 138 episodes) and notes about episode lengths, live episodes, and special formats are provided as factual standards of the show's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filming location and set construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Filmed in New York (mostly at Silvercup Studios); the show often built elaborate sets (one set took three days to build for six seconds of screen time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location and set-production choices are described as part of production values and practical considerations in making the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble cast and character roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Features an ensemble cast; seven roles receive star billing in opening credits; recurring cast and guest stars bolster episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article details primary and recurring characters, their archetypes and dynamics (e.g., Liz vs. Jack ideological tension), which function as criteria for evaluating performance and ensemble effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and original songs (score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features a 'jaunty' jazz score composed by Jeff Richmond; theme music was Emmy-nominated; seven short original songs appeared in episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original music and songs are discussed as part of the show's production craft and contributed to its critical recognition (example: theme nomination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of celebrity guest stars and real-life cameos
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous guest stars and real-life politician cameos (e.g., Al Gore, Nancy Pelosi) appeared on the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guest appearances are treated as notable production/casting choices that influenced episodes and public reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality and engagement with real events
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictionalizes or parodies real-world industry events (e.g., NBCUniversal acquisition; story arcs reflecting network mergers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The show's engagement with contemporary media-business topics is documented as part of its satirical remit and subject matter relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical acclaim and industry awards as success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: 30 Rock won multiple major awards (Primetime Emmys for Outstanding Comedy Series in 2007, 2008, 2009; nominated 103 Primetime Emmy Awards, won 16) and appeared on many critics' year-end 'best of' lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses awards, nomination counts, critics' lists, and rankings (Writers Guild, Peabody, Golden Globes, etc.) to summarize the series' industry recognition and critical stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience ratings versus critical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite critical acclaim, the series struggled in the ratings throughout its run (pilot generated 8.13 million viewers; varied season averages noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratings data (Nielsen figures, DVR viewing percentages, season-by-season viewership) are presented as a contrasting metric to critical success, indicating multiple axes for evaluating a show's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and responses to controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Received recognition from GLAAD for LGBT portrayal; in 2020 four episodes featuring actors in blackface were removed from streaming at the creators' request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents both praise for representation and later ethical/creative decisions (episode removals) — these are presented as factors in evaluating the show's cultural responsibility and legacy.
